Foundation models · Block 1

Foundation models, scaling and in-context learning

A pretrained encoder can support several tasks. A generative language model can also use a task instruction and examples in its input. This page explains how that process works, how to evaluate it, and how model size and training data share a compute budget.

Microlecture 1

What is a foundation model?

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

A pretrained model can support several tasks. BERT illustrates this reuse with an encoder and task-specific heads. A decoder-only language model can instead generate a sentiment label, an inference label or a list of entities as text. Foundation-model reuse includes both model families.

For a decoder-only model, each task request can use the same pretrained decoder and language-model head. The prompt specifies the task and output format. During prompting, the model weights stay fixed. Fine-tuning uses task data to change selected weights. These are different ways to reuse a pretrained model.

A foundation model is trained on broad data at scale and can be adapted to many downstream tasks. A downstream task is a task for which we reuse the pretrained model. The term describes a training-and-reuse approach. It includes encoder models such as BERT and generative language models. It also extends beyond text.

One model, several uses

Pretraining: learn representations from a broad text corpus.
Reuse: classify a review, compare two sentences, or identify person names.
Task evaluation: check each use on suitable labelled examples.

Compare this with a classifier trained only on labelled movie reviews. That system learns a direct route to one label set. Broad pretraining separates much of the representation learning from the choice of task. Task-specific training may still be needed.

A foundation model is not automatically a chat assistant. For example, BERT supplies contextual representations and masked-token predictions. A conversational interface requires further choices about training, input format and output behaviour.

Broad reuse is a useful starting point. It does not establish equal performance on every task. A model can also pass errors from its pretraining into several applications.

Sources: J&M §1.2, pp. 8–11; Chapter 7 Historical Notes, p. 207. Bommasani et al., §1.

Review from the previous lecture

Using a language model for a task

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI-only review. No instructor video or slides are available for this section.

This review brings together task-specific classification, encoder adaptation and generation through a language-model head. Use it to check the distinction between the output interface and parameter updates. The worked examples and practice questions remain available below.

Use one input throughout this comparison: “The film was wonderful.” Our target label is Positive. We can obtain a label through different training routes and output interfaces.

Three methods for the same sentiment task
MethodBefore task inferenceOutput
Task-specific classifierTrain logistic regression on word features, such as TF–IDF, using labelled reviews.A score for each sentiment label.
Fine-tune a pretrained encoderAdd a task head. Train it on labelled reviews; update selected encoder parameters or the full encoder as specified.A score for each sentiment label.
Prompt a generative language modelPut the instruction and review in the context. Use the chosen model without a task-specific parameter update.Text such as “Positive”, using the vocabulary head.

A task head maps a representation to task labels. For a BERT three-class classifier, the final vector for [CLS] is a row vector of length d. With biases omitted:

ŷ = softmax(hLCLS WC),   WC ∈ ℝd × 3.

A generative language model instead scores vocabulary tokens. In a tied-weight example, the vocabulary logits are hEᵀ, where Eᵀ has shape d × |V|. Softmax gives the next-token distribution. A label written as text can contain more than one token.

Conditional generation

Classify the review as Positive, Negative or Neutral.
Review: The film was wonderful.
Sentiment:

The model generates a continuation, for example Positive. This is an intended response, not a measured model result.

Write the prompt as x and the generated response as tokens y₁,…,yₘ. The model assigns Pθ(y | x) = ∏t=1m Pθ(yt | x, y<t). Each generated token becomes part of the context for the next prediction.

Head choice and parameter updates are separate decisions. A frozen encoder can support a trained head. A generative model can also be fine-tuned. Here, “prompting” means inference without a parameter update. Supervised fine-tuning uses labelled examples to change selected model parameters.

Further detail: BERT’s vocabulary head

BERT can score label words at a masked position, such as “It was [MASK].” Its MLM head applies a transform before vocabulary projection: use zEᵀ, where z is the transformed vector. This differs from the simple causal-model example above. Pattern-Exploiting Training (PET) uses patterns and label words and includes fine-tuning; it is not an example of purely fixed-weight prompting. See Schick and Schütze, §§3–3.1.

Sources: J&M §9.4.1, pp. 236–237; §7.5, pp. 193–195; §1.7, pp. 21–24.

Microlecture 3

Zero-shot and few-shot prompting

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

A generative language model uses its vocabulary head to produce task responses as token sequences. We now keep that model fixed and change the information in its prompt. The output-head review explains the distinction from a classifier over task labels.

An instruction states what to do. A demonstration is a completed input–output example in the prompt. The new input is the instance that the model must answer.

Zero-shot prompting supplies no demonstrations. One-shot prompting supplies one. Few-shot prompting supplies a small set. These counts describe examples in the current context. They do not count examples seen during pretraining.

Zero-shot: no demonstrations

Classify each review as Positive, Negative or Neutral.
Return only the label.
Review: The film was wonderful.
Sentiment:

Few-shot: two demonstrations

Classify each review as Positive, Negative or Neutral.
Return only the label.
Review: I enjoyed every minute.
Sentiment: Positive
Review: The plot was dull.
Sentiment: Negative
Review: The film was wonderful.
Sentiment:

The instruction and final review are matched across these prompts. Only the demonstrations differ. The final unfinished review is not a demonstration. In both cases, the model is expected to generate Positive. We must run an evaluation to know whether it does so reliably.

Neither demonstration shows Neutral. Demonstrations can help specify the meaning of the labels they include. Neutral has no demonstration here. The model must interpret it from the instruction, pretrained knowledge and the surrounding context.

J&M Fig. 1.14 gives a one-shot computer-science example. One solved asymptotic-complexity question is followed by a Python string-concatenation question. The solved example shows the question format and the required answer format. The model still has to answer the new question.

Demonstrations can specify label meanings, input structure and output style. Their usefulness depends on the model and task. More demonstrations also occupy more context; their count alone does not guarantee better answers.

In the translation example, a completed pair such as “sea otter ⇒ loutre de mer” is a demonstration. The final “cheese ⇒” is the query. The number of earlier pairs determines the shot count. The task description can remain fixed while the examples change.

Sources: J&M §1.7, pp. 21–22, especially Fig. 1.14.

Microlecture 4

In-context learning

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

Consider the one-shot prompt in the textbook. The complete context ends at the final Answer:. The response is generated after that boundary.

Context supplied to the model · J&M Fig. 1.14

The following are questions about high school computer science.

Which is the largest asymptotically?
(A) O(1) (B) O(n) (C) O(n²) (D) O(log(n))
Answer: C

What is the output of the statement “a” + “ab” in Python 3?
(A) Error (B) aab (C) ab (D) a ab
Answer:

Intended completion

B

The first question and Answer: C form one demonstration. The second question is the new input. Python concatenates the two strings to form aab, so the correct choice is B.

During the forward computation, the prompt changes token representations, attention outputs and the next-token distribution. The instruction and solved example give evidence about the task and answer format. The parameter values θ remain fixed during this inference process.

In-context learning (ICL) is task behaviour conditioned on instructions or examples in the context, without a parameter update during the stated inference process. “Learning” here describes use of the context. It does not imply that the prompt has been stored permanently in the weights.

A diagnostic comparison
OperationWhat changes?What is retained?
Add a solved example to a prompt.Context, activations and output probabilities.The example can influence predictions while it remains in the supplied context.
Fine-tune on labelled examples.Trainable parameters through gradient updates.The updated parameters can be used on later inputs without including those training examples.

Removing a demonstration from the supplied context removes that input evidence. It does not erase pretraining knowledge, and the model may still give the same answer. Include the demonstration in a later query if you want it in that query’s context. Fine-tuned parameters remain changed without including the training examples in each later prompt.

Context computation also occurs in pretraining forward passes. The training procedure additionally computes gradients and updates parameters. During the inference process described here, in-context learning performs no such parameter update.

Read this graph within one curve first. The model stays fixed, and the horizontal axis changes the number of examples in its input. The vertical axis is task accuracy. In this symbol-removal task, the larger model benefits more from added examples. Comparing colours also changes model size. The graph therefore supports a result for these models and this task; it does not establish that every extra example helps every model.

Sources: J&M §1.7 and §1.7.1, pp. 21–24; §7.5 for vocabulary prediction; §§8.1 and 9.4.1 for fine-tuning.

Microlecture 5

Pretraining and task reuse

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

Documents can contain repeated structures: question–answer lists, translation pairs or worked calculations. Within such a training document, earlier items can help predict a later item. Brown et al. use the following arithmetic schematic to illustrate this possibility.

Within a sequence: earlier tokens affect later predictions through the forward pass. Across training batches: prediction losses supply gradients for parameter updates. Context computation occurs in both training and inference; only the training procedure applies these updates.

The same kind of structure can appear in two settings. Within a training document, earlier items can help predict a later item, and the prediction loss can reward useful context use. At inference, a prompt with demonstrations can present a similar structure. The model can reuse context-use skills learned during pretraining, with no parameter update. This does not establish that every task uses the same internal mechanism.

A token-loss illustration · assumed probabilities

For the correct next token, use ℓt = −ln Pθ(wt | w<t).

Probability of the correct tokenLoss, in nats
0.10−ln(0.10) ≈ 2.303
0.50−ln(0.50) ≈ 0.693

These values illustrate the loss formula. They are not model measurements.

If context raises the correct token’s probability, its loss falls. Pretraining can therefore favour useful context use. This is a training motivation. It does not provide a complete mechanism for ICL.

Brown et al. leave open whether a model learns a new task at inference or recognises patterns from pretraining. A successful completion alone does not distinguish those explanations.

Sources: J&M §7.7, pp. 201–203. Brown et al., §1, Fig. 1.1 and footnote 1.

Optional aside

How does context help if the weights never change?

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI-only optional aside. No instructor video or slides are available for this section.

Microlecture 4 showed that a demonstration can change the output while θ stays fixed. Microlecture 5 gave a training reason for useful context use. This aside asks what happens during the forward pass. It goes beyond the textbook: treat each research result below as evidence in particular settings.

A fixed function of its input

The model computes Pθ(next token | context). Fixing θ fixes the function, not its output. A least-squares solver is a useful comparison. Its code stays the same, yet more data points change the fitted line. In this comparison, the model weights play the role of the solver, and the demonstrations supply data. Context-dependent information is represented in activations. Autoregressive generation uses successive forward computations and can retain attention keys and values in a cache. No parameter update from the demonstrations persists into a fresh inference computation. Information derived from them can still be present in generated text or a retained cache.

Attention reads the context

At a token position, each causal attention head compares a query with keys at allowed positions, including earlier tokens. It then mixes their values using the resulting weights. Consider the final Answer: in the J&M Fig. 1.14 prompt. As an illustration, a head could attend to the earlier Answer: or its following C. Information from these positions could help specify the answer format: a single capital letter. Other computations could combine this format information with the new question. This is a schematic explanation of how attention could help. It is not a measured attention pattern or an identified circuit for this prompt.

Olsson et al. describe induction heads: attention heads that can match an earlier occurrence of a token and promote the token that followed it. Their basic pattern is [A][B] … [A] → [B]. In “sea otter ⇒ loutre … sea otter ⇒”, this kind of pattern could help continue with the token or tokens for “loutre”; the complete response can involve several heads and layers. In the models studied, induction heads formed near a sharp improvement in in-context learning. The paper gives strong causal evidence in small attention-only models and correlational evidence in larger models with feed-forward layers. Copying a repeat is one mechanism, not a complete account.

Three views of what demonstrations add

  • Evidence about the task. Xie et al. treat pretraining documents as drawn from many latent tasks. The prompt acts as evidence that sharpens a posterior over those tasks, and the prediction follows the inferred task.
  • Learning in the activations. In controlled linear-regression settings, transformers trained on many tasks can implement steps equivalent to gradient descent on the demonstrations, inside the forward pass (von Oswald et al.; Akyürek et al.). These results do not establish the same mechanism in large language models.
  • What demonstrations supply. Min et al. replaced correct labels in demonstrations with random labels; on many classification tasks, accuracy fell only slightly. The format, the label set and the kind of input mattered more. Wei et al. found that sufficiently large models can follow flipped labels, so the role of demonstrations changes with scale.

In one sentence: pretraining turns the weights into a general procedure for using context, and at inference the demonstrations are input to that procedure. Activations and output probabilities change while θ stays the same. None of these accounts is a complete explanation of in-context learning in large models, so claims about a prompt still need the evaluation of Microlecture 6.

Sources: J&M Ch. 7 for attention. Olsson et al.; Xie et al.; von Oswald et al.; Akyürek et al.; Min et al.; Wei et al.

Self-study questions
  1. Explain how a model with fixed weights can give a different answer when a demonstration is added. Use either the solver comparison or the attention mechanism.
  2. Min et al. found that random labels in demonstrations reduced accuracy less than expected. Give one explanation, and one reason the result may change for larger models.

Microlecture 6

Evaluating prompts and demonstrations

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

A useful example is not yet evidence of reliable performance. Compare prompts on held-out inputs: examples whose answers were not used as demonstrations for those predictions. Use a development set to choose a prompt. Reserve a separate final test set for the chosen method.

For sentiment classification, fix the label set and the scoring rule before comparison. For example, accept exactly one of Positive, Negative or Neutral, after trimming surrounding spaces. Count any other output as invalid and incorrect. Inspect invalid outputs separately.

Applying the rule · invented outputs, not model results

InputReference labelModel outputScore
I loved it.PositivePositiveCorrect
It was awful.NegativeNeutralValid, incorrect
A great film.PositiveSentiment: PositiveInvalid, incorrect

Accuracy = 1/3. Valid outputs = 2/3. Invalid outputs = 1/3.

Now suppose a revised prompt stops the model from writing the prefix. The scoring rule stays unchanged. The third output becomes Positive, so accuracy rises to 2/3. The Neutral answer for a negative review is still wrong: the format improved, but the sentiment error did not.

A lenient parser that accepted Sentiment: Positive would also give 2/3 here. Strict or lenient matching is a choice. Make it once, before comparing prompts, and apply it to every prompt.

A controlled experiment to run · no results are claimed
ConditionChange from the baselinePurpose
AZero-shot instruction.Establish the baseline.
BAdd two fixed, labelled training examples.Test the effect of those demonstrations.
CReverse only their order.Test sensitivity to order.
DChange only the instruction wording in B.Test sensitivity to wording.

Use the same model version, held-out inputs, decoding settings and scoring code for each development comparison. Keep demonstrations separate from the evaluated inputs. To study demonstration choice, repeat B with another declared pair while holding the remaining choices fixed.

If generation uses sampling, repeat the runs with declared seeds where supported. Report the mean accuracy and the range or spread. Also report the number of test inputs, invalid outputs and the main error types. A fixed seed can aid reproducibility; it does not prove that the result generalises.

A finite test set introduces sampling uncertainty even when generation is deterministic. For 100 independent test inputs sampled from the target population and accuracy near 75%, the estimated standard error of one accuracy figure is √(0.75 × 0.25 / 100) ≈ 0.043, or 4.3 percentage points. One standard error is not a 95% confidence interval. A simple normal approximation gives a 95% interval of about 75% ± 8.5 percentage points. This interval describes uncertainty in one accuracy estimate. It does not give a cutoff for a difference between prompts. When two prompts use the same test inputs, compare their predictions as paired observations. A paired bootstrap can estimate uncertainty in the accuracy difference; McNemar’s test uses the inputs on which their correctness differs. Report the difference and its uncertainty before judging the evidence for an improvement.

Select the prompt using development results. Then lock the prompt, demonstrations and scoring rule before final testing. Repeatedly revising a prompt after seeing final test answers turns that set into selection data.

Choosing on the test set · a simulation, not model results

Suppose 20 prompts are equally good, each with a true accuracy of 0.75, and each is scored on 100 test inputs with independent sampling noise. The measured scores scatter around 0.75. Averaged over many simulated draws, the best of the 20 scores about 0.83: roughly 8 points above the truth, although no prompt is better.

Reporting that winner’s test score overstates its accuracy. A fresh final test set removes this selection effect.

A prompt can improve formatting while leaving sentiment errors unchanged. Record both. This protocol tests specific prompt choices; it does not establish that all few-shot prompts outperform zero-shot prompts.

Sources: J&M §1.7 for demonstrations; §1.9, pp. 25–29, for task evaluation. The controlled comparison below specifies one evaluation protocol.

Microlecture 7

Model size, data and compute

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

Prompt comparisons hold the model fixed. Scaling studies compare training runs. They ask how prediction loss changes as we vary the resources used to train a model.

Quantities used in the scaling comparison
SymbolMeaningUnit or convention
NModel parameter count.Parameters. State whether embeddings are counted; the Chinchilla study counts all parameters.
DTokens processed during training.Token presentations. Seeing the same token again adds another presentation.
CTraining computation.Floating-point operations (FLOPs). This is an operation count, not a duration.
LMean next-token prediction loss.Nats per token when the natural logarithm is used.

For a dense Transformer, a common rough training estimate is C ≈ 6ND. The factor six approximates the forward and backward matrix computations. Per token, each parameter takes part in about one multiplication and one addition in the forward pass: about 2N FLOPs. The backward pass costs about twice as much, 4N. Together they give about 6N FLOPs per token, or 6ND for D tokens. Attention, embeddings and system costs can require a more detailed estimate. We will use this approximation in the worked comparison below.

A scaling curve relates a specified loss to size, tokens or compute under a stated training setup. It can show predictable trends over a measured range. A fitted power law is an empirical description within assumptions and a range; it is not a guarantee for every future model.

The nearly straight line illustrates a power law on logarithmic axes. The plot’s N counts non-embedding parameters. This differs from the all-parameter convention used in the Chinchilla allocation discussion. State the counting convention when comparing fits. The exponent shown here describes loss versus model size; it is a different quantity from the compute-allocation exponents discussed below.

Kaplan et al. fit L = (N / (8.8 × 10¹³))−0.076. Each tenfold increase in N multiplies the fitted loss by 10−0.076 ≈ 0.84. The ratio stays the same, but the absolute gain shrinks: from 10⁵ to 10⁷ parameters the fitted loss falls by about 1.4 nats; from 10⁷ to 10⁹, by about 1.0 nat.

A simple comparison

Run A has 10 billion parameters and sees 200 billion tokens.
Run B has 20 billion parameters and sees 100 billion tokens.
Both give C ≈ 1.2 × 10²² FLOPs under the same estimate.

Equal estimated compute permits different losses. We need measurements or a validated loss model to rank the runs.

Use comparable data distributions, tokenizers and loss definitions. Repetition increases D without adding the same amount of new information. Data quality, duplication and evaluation contamination can change the meaning of a comparison.

Repeated passes through a fixed corpus

A fixed corpus contains 10 billion tokens. Three complete passes produce 30 billion token presentations: 10 billion × 3 = 30 billion.

The training token count D increases, while the amount of distinct text stays the same.

Loss is counted per token, so the tokenizer must match before losses are compared.

Why the tokenizer must match · illustrative numbers

Suppose one sentence costs 24 nats in total. A tokenizer that splits it into 8 tokens reports 24 / 8 = 3.0 nats per token. A tokenizer that splits it into 12 tokens reports 24 / 12 = 2.0 nats per token. The prediction is no better; only the token count changed.

For a fixed tokenizer and test set, lower mean next-token loss means better prediction of that text; perplexity is exp(L). For example, L = 2.4 nats per token, near the largest models in the Kaplan figure, gives exp(2.4) ≈ 11: as uncertain as a choice among 11 equally likely tokens. Task accuracy and the factual reliability of generated claims need their own checks. A lower pretraining loss does not guarantee improvement on every task.

Sources: J&M §1.1, p. 7; §7.7 and §7.7.1, pp. 201–203; §7.8, pp. 204–205. Scaling plots are research extensions.

Given one compute budget, how should we divide it between parameters and training tokens?

Microlecture 8

Allocating a training budget

InstructorVideo · Slides (PDF)

AI versionVideo · Slides (PDF)

Models in the scaling study

Gopher and Chinchilla are pretrained language models from DeepMind. Both use dense decoder-only Transformers and learn through next-token prediction.

Gopher was introduced in 2021, with 280 billion parameters and 300 billion training tokens. Chinchilla was introduced in 2022, with 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion training tokens. The later model was informed by experiments on how to allocate training compute.

The research question is concrete: could a smaller model, trained on more tokens, perform better at a comparable training budget? The experiments below explain how the researchers investigated this question.

Benchmarks and task accuracy

A benchmark provides shared test questions or tasks. To interpret a reported result, also state the scoring rule and the evaluation procedure.

MMLU means Massive Multitask Language Understanding. It contains multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, including mathematics, medicine, law and computer science. Accuracy measures the percentage of answers that are correct. The Gopher–Chinchilla comparison reports mean accuracy across these subjects.

The reported results use a five-shot protocol: the prompt contains five solved demonstrations, followed by a new question that the model must answer. Keep the demonstrations separate from the test questions. State the prompt protocol when comparing scores.

J&M also introduces other benchmarks in §1.9.1 and Fig. 1.18:

  • BIG-Bench Hard: challenging reasoning tasks.
  • GSM8K: school mathematics problems.
  • AIME24: competition mathematics questions from the 2024 examination.

Use the same test questions, scoring rule and prompt protocol for a controlled comparison. Check for overlap between training data and test questions. Such overlap can inflate the reported score. These task scores measure a different aspect of performance from next-token prediction loss.

A larger model uses more training compute per token. Under a fixed budget, increasing N therefore reduces the token count we can afford. Hoffmann et al. studied this trade-off by varying both quantities.

Their experiments support increasing model size and training tokens in roughly equal proportions as compute grows. The familiar D ≈ 20N rule is a rounded summary of their compute-optimal training estimates. It means about 20 training tokens per parameter under those conditions. It is not an exact constant across all settings.

Worked allocation · illustrative budget and rounded rule

Let C = 1.2 × 10²² FLOPs. Assume a dense Transformer, C ≈ 6ND and D ≈ 20N.

C ≈ 120N²
N ≈ √(C/120) = √(10²⁰) = 10¹⁰ parameters
D ≈ 20 × 10¹⁰ = 2 × 10¹¹ tokens

This gives 10 billion parameters and 200 billion training tokens. Checking: 6 × (10 × 10⁹) × (200 × 10⁹) = 1.2 × 10²² FLOPs.

This is Run A from the previous section. Run B uses the same estimated compute, but has 5 tokens per parameter. The rounded allocation rule favours A under its assumptions. We have not measured the losses of these two illustrative runs.

If the budget is four times larger and the same approximations apply, double N and D: 20 billion parameters and 400 billion tokens use about 4.8 × 10²² FLOPs. Doubling both quantities multiplies their product by four.

The paper’s large-scale comparison used Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, against Gopher, with 280 billion parameters and 300 billion tokens, at the same reported training compute. Chinchilla has a quarter of Gopher’s parameters and about 4.7 times as many training tokens. Its ratio, 1.4 trillion / 70 billion, is exactly 20 tokens per parameter; Gopher has about 1.

On five-shot MMLU, Gopher scored 60.0% and Chinchilla 67.6%: 7.6 percentage points higher in mean accuracy (Hoffmann et al., Table 6). This is an empirical comparison, not a controlled one. The optimizer, tokenizer and training-data mixture also changed.

Checking “same compute” with C ≈ 6ND

Gopher: 6 × (280 × 10⁹) × (300 × 10⁹) ≈ 5.0 × 10²³ FLOPs.
Chinchilla: 6 × (70 × 10⁹) × (1.4 × 10¹²) ≈ 5.9 × 10²³ FLOPs.

The paper describes comparable reported training budgets. Its numerical values use different FLOP-counting conventions. Table 3 uses 5.76 × 10²³ FLOPs as the Gopher budget. Appendix F revises the earlier Gopher calculation to 6.3 × 10²³ FLOPs using a more detailed count. These are not two model budgets to compare against each other. State the counting convention when quoting a budget. The 6ND estimate is a rough guide; it does not reproduce every term in the paper’s accounting.

Training optimum and deployment

Compute-optimal training minimises the study’s loss for a training budget. Deployment also involves inference cost, latency, available data and the number of future uses. These can justify a different allocation. The 20-token rule is not a universal deployment prescription.

Serving cost · a rough estimate from the same approximations

For a dense model, the main parameter-matrix computations in a forward pass cost about 2N FLOPs per token. With cached attention keys and values, this gives a rough cost per generated token. Under this approximation, Gopher costs about 5.6 × 10¹¹ FLOPs and Chinchilla about 1.4 × 10¹¹: a quarter as much. This estimate omits context-length-dependent attention computations and system overheads. It is an operation count, not a direct estimate of latency or monetary cost.

Let T be the total number of tokens processed during inference, including prompt tokens and generated tokens. Under the same approximation, inference costs about 2NT. This equals the training cost 6ND when T = 3D. For Chinchilla, that is about 3 × 1.4 trillion = 4.2 trillion processed tokens. If lifetime inference usage exceeds this threshold, inference compute exceeds training compute under these assumptions. Counting only generated tokens would omit prompt-processing costs. Context-dependent attention and system costs can also change the comparison. An objective that includes lifetime inference cost can therefore favour a smaller model trained on more tokens than the training-only optimum.

Further detail: scaling fits and exponents

Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. estimated different compute allocations from different experiments. In Hoffmann et al. Table 2, the fitted exponents in Nopt ∝ Ca and Dopt ∝ Cb are 0.50/0.50, 0.49/0.51 and 0.46/0.54 for their three approaches. “Roughly equal” allows these differences. The same table lists the earlier Kaplan et al. estimates, a ≈ 0.73 and b ≈ 0.27, which direct most additional compute to parameters. Models of the Gopher era were sized in that spirit. See Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. §§3.1–3.4.

Sources: J&M §1.1, p. 7; §1.9.1, pp. 25–26, Fig. 1.18. Rae et al.: Gopher. Hendrycks et al.: MMLU. Hoffmann et al., §§3.1–3.4, Fig. 3 and Table 3; §4 and Tables 1 and 6.

Quick questions · 3 MCQs and 2 MSQs

Five questions: 3 MCQs and 2 MSQs. An MSQ is correct only when you select all correct options and no extras. Scores are for self-checking.

Self-study questions
  1. Repeat the allocation calculation for C = 3 × 10²¹ FLOPs using the same two approximations.
  2. Explain why a model serving billions of requests might use a different training allocation from the training-only optimum.
  3. Name two assumptions that you would check before using a published scaling fit.

The next question is how to adapt a pretrained model with labelled examples. Supervised fine-tuning changes selected parameters. Parameter-efficient methods, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA), reduce the number of parameters that must be trained.

Back to topics

Block 1

Block 1 recap

  • Pretraining and reuse. Broad pretraining supports reuse across tasks. Prediction loss can favour the use of earlier context.
  • Prompting and in-context learning. Instructions and demonstrations specify the task. Inference changes activations while model weights stay fixed.
  • Evaluation. Use development data for prompt selection and a separate final test. State the scoring rule and prompt protocol for benchmark comparisons.
  • Scaling. Model size and training tokens must fit the compute budget. Scaling fits describe results under a stated training setup. Compute-optimal allocation grows parameters and tokens together; deployment cost can favour a smaller model trained on more tokens.

Sources and further study

Textbook: Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin, Speech and Language Processing, August 2026 draft. The references below use its section numbers and printed page numbers.

  • §1.2, “What do LLMs Learn From Word (Token) Prediction?”, pp. 8–11: broad knowledge acquired through prediction. Foundation-model terminology also appears in Chapter 7 Historical Notes, p. 207.
  • §1.7, “Inference”, pp. 21–24, including §1.7.1 and Fig. 1.14: prompts, demonstrations and fixed-weight context use. §1.9, pp. 25–29: task evaluation.
  • §7.5, “The Language Modeling Head”, pp. 193–195: vocabulary predictions. §7.7, “Pretraining Transformer LLMs”, pp. 201–203, including §7.7.1: loss and perplexity. §7.8, “Current models and some numbers”, pp. 204–205: scale and architecture quantities.
  • §9.4.1, “Sequence Classification”, pp. 236–237: the BERT classifier head and Eq. 9.6. §1.1, p. 7: parameters and the broad scaling summary.

Research papers

  • Bommasani et al. (2021), On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models, §1: broad training and adaptation to downstream tasks.
  • Brown et al. (2020), Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, §1, Fig. 1.1 and footnote 1: the repeated-task schematic and the distinction between task learning and pattern recognition.
  • Rae et al. (2021), Scaling Language Models: Methods, Analysis & Insights from Training Gopher: the Gopher model and its evaluations.
  • Hendrycks et al. (2021), Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding, §§3–4: the benchmark, subjects and few-shot protocol.
  • Hoffmann et al. (2022), Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, §§3.1–3.4, Fig. 3, Tables 2–3: allocation and empirical fits; §4, Tables 1 and 6: Chinchilla and Gopher; Appendix F: FLOP counting.
  • Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. Comparison with the later Chinchilla fits.
  • Olsson et al. (2022), In-context Learning and Induction Heads: induction heads and their link to in-context learning.
  • Xie et al. (2022), An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference: in-context learning as inference over latent tasks.
  • von Oswald et al. (2023), Transformers Learn In-Context by Gradient Descent: gradient-descent-like steps in the forward pass, in controlled settings.
  • Akyürek et al. (2023), What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning? Investigations with Linear Models: learning algorithms implemented in context for linear regression.
  • Min et al. (2022), Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?: the effect of label correctness, format and input distribution.
  • Wei et al. (2023), Larger Language Models Do In-Context Learning Differently: flipped labels and the effect of scale.
  • Schick and Schütze (2021), Exploiting Cloze-Questions for Few-Shot Text Classification and Natural Language Inference, §§3–3.1. Pattern/verbalizer methods. BERT MLM implementation: original run_pretraining.py, get_masked_lm_output.
